steps.title: Popliteal Fossa
steps.body: The popliteal fossa is the posterior knee diamond. Its main contents from superficial to deep are tibial nerve, popliteal vein, and popliteal artery.

steps.title: Relationships and functional organization
steps.body: Superolateral boundary: biceps femoris. Superomedial boundary: semimembranosus and semitendinosus. Inferolateral boundary: lateral head of gastrocnemius. Inferomedial boundary: medial head of gastrocnemius. Floor: femur, posterior capsule, popliteus. Also contains common fibular nerve laterally, small saphenous vein termination, popliteal lymph nodes, and fat.

steps.title: Why can the common fibular nerve be affected near the fibular neck rather than centrally in the fossa?
steps.body: The nerve follows the lateral border along biceps femoris and then winds around the fibular neck, where its superficial course makes it anatomically exposed. It later divides into deep and superficial branches for anterior and lateral leg compartments. The tibial nerve instead continues centrally and into posterior leg routes. A lesion near the neck can therefore involve two distal compartments while sparing tibial targets. Follow the nerve beyond the fossa boundary to connect local course with distal function.

steps.title: Apply the anatomy and resolve a common confusion
steps.body: The artery lies deepest against the fossa floor, while the tibial nerve is most superficial in the central bundle. The common fibular nerve follows the lateral boundary toward the fibular neck rather than remaining central. Gastrocnemius and hamstring borders frame the diamond-shaped region. Depth matters when identifying a structure on dissection or an image: a vessel's pulsation does not imply it is the most superficial structure. Trace continuity above and below the knee to confirm identity.
